  • A big pot with a lid that lets steam escape. Water will need to escape. I use a crock pot because I don't want to sit and watch it all day but it takes 1 day or more with the temperatures of my crockpot. I can also set the crockpot in a place where there is little risk of it spilling on someone.

  • A funnel

  • Cheesecloth. I recommend this over a fine sieve because degreasing sieves is a pain in the ass. A small square of cheesecloth is more than enough and can be tossed afterwards.

  • A mason jar or other container. *You need to know it won't break or leak from the heat.

  • A laddle with no holes

  • Something to catch drips Preventing a mess is better than cleaning it up.

Okay, what do?

  • Give the fats a rinse if using fresh. If using frozen don't worry about thawing. Throw them in your pot with about 1/4 inch of water. The water is to prevent burning.

  • You want to achieve a steady simmer. At this point you want to make sure all the steam (water) can escape as your material comes to temperature. Leave the lid propped open if you feel water is lingering. It can take several hours for the water to cook out because the meat and fat also contain water. Just be patient.

  • Prepare your work space so you can start laddling the oil into your jar. I like to put the jar on a plate. Cover Jar opening with cheesecloth. Use wide mouth funnel to secure cheesecloth.

  • Laddle out the oil. As the day goes on, more and more oil will cook out of the fatty bits. Eventually, you'll be able to spoon it out. Just let the oil flow into the laddle and into the funnel you pour. Try to avoid scoping out meaty pieces. Once the oil is coming out very steady, I usually will laddle every hour.

  • (Note) If you are doing this the super slow way in a crockpot, turn it to keep warm when you go to sleep. Oil can burn and catch fire. Be safe

  • Many hours, possibly days later, your meaty bits will stop releasing oil. You'll be left with some burnt-ish crispy pieces. Remove them and let them sit in a stainer. Remove and filter the last of the oil from your pot.

  • (Note) The left over crispy bits are called cracklings. They are very edible and can be seasoned like potato chips. Beef makes a more jerky like crackling. Crackling cornbread is what my southern grannies used to make.

Made the stuff...what's next?

The most obvious thing is to cook with it. You can fry, bake, make sauces, etc. Some examples of other uses:

  • Making Soap
  • Tanning hides because this was considered woman's work in my grannies' days
  • Making animal feed

That's it. You have eliminated waste and made something you know is not toxic to your family. Humans need animal fats in our diets not soybean oil. I got a quart of tallow from this and it will last us about 3-4 months. If you are a fryer like I am, regularly clean and filter you oil so you can reuse it.
